### USER

AI-Scientist-v2 — Deep-Dive Runbook (Report #2)
Goal this round (per Taiming's feedback): stop surveying breadth, go deep on one or two
representative agent failures. For each: reconstruct what the agent actually tried, find where it
got stuck, classify the root cause (task spec / model capability / tool-use strategy), and propose
an intervention. Then frame why this system exists and what gap it fills. Most of the value is in
thinking, not in running more jobs — so a lot of this is mining logs you already have plus 1–2
clean controlled experiments.
Ground rules — stay inside the real source, don't improvise.
Everything here must run on the actual AI-Scientist-v2 repository and be reasoned about from the
actual paper. Do not invent scripts, flags, config keys, or behavior that aren't in the repo,
and don't paraphrase the paper from memory — work from the real text.
Code (the only source of truth for commands/args/config): https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2
Paper (the only source of truth for claims/framing): https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.08066) — also linked from the repo as https://pub.sakana.ai/ai-scientist-v2/paper
When using Claude Code: point it at the cloned repo and the paper, and tell it to read the
actual files before acting — e.g. "Read launch_scientist_bfts.py and bfts_config.yaml in this
repo and only use flags/keys that actually exist there; if something I asked for isn't in the
code, tell me instead of inventing it." If a command in this runbook ever disagrees with the
repo's current README, the repo wins — verify against the repo.
Part A — Conceptual framing (the "why this exists / what gap" section)
Taiming wants you to reason about the paper, not just the code. AI-Scientist-v2 isn't a benchmark
in the SWE-bench sense — but it is an evaluation claim: the "score" is whether an end-to-end
agent can produce a paper that passes real peer review. Frame it along these lines (answer in your
own words — these are prompts, not answers to copy):
What is the actual evaluation signal? The headline result is "first entirely AI-generated
paper accepted at an ICLR workshop." Is peer-review acceptance a good proxy for scientific
value? What does it over-reward (polish, framing, figure aesthetics) vs under-reward (genuine
novelty, correctness)? Note the VLM reviewer loop refines figure aesthetics — interesting
signal about what "acceptable" optimizes for.
Gap vs v1 (arXiv:2408.06292). v1 relied on human-authored per-domain code templates →
high success but narrow and non-generalizing. v2 removes templates, generalizes across ML
domains, and uses progressive agentic tree search managed by an experiment-manager agent →
broader and more open-ended, but lower success. The README itself admits v2 isn't strictly
"better." So: is removing scaffolding always progress? When does structure help vs constrain?
Gap vs closed agent benchmarks (SWE-bench, MLE-bench, RE-bench). Those grade well-specified
tasks with known solutions and automatic checks. AI-Scientist-v2 targets open-ended discovery
with no ground-truth solution. That's the gap it fills — and also why it's hard to measure. The
tree search + experiment manager is the mechanism for searching an open solution space rather
than solving a closed one.
Where it sits among peers (for the related-work paragraph): AlphaEvolve (2506.13131,
algorithmic discovery), AI co-scientist (2502.18864, hypothesis generation), Kosmos
(2511.02824). v2's distinctive bet is full end-to-end with the artifact being a peer-reviewed
paper.
Tie it to your failure cases. End the section with: from what you observed, is the
bottleneck ideation, execution (tool use), or evaluation? Which would you invest in? (This is
the bridge Taiming hinted at — "sometimes research ideas come from this.")
Reading list (in priority order):
AI-Scientist-v2 paper — arXiv:2504.08066 (read Table 1: v1-vs-v2 comparison, and the tree-search section)
AI-Scientist v1 — arXiv:2408.06292 (to feel the template approach you're contrasting against)
AIDE (github.com/WecoAI/aideml) — the tree search component is built on this; skim how nodes/debug work
Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts — arXiv:2601.03315
(excellent failure-mode vocabulary; great to cite in your diagnosis section)
Optional contrast: AlphaEvolve (2506.13131), AI co-scientist (2502.18864)
Part B — Mine the logs you already have (free, do this first)
You don't need new runs to start the deep-dive. Every run wrote a timestamped folder under
experiments/. The tree search produces nodes; failed nodes are where the diagnosis lives.
Where to look:
experiments/<timestamp_ideaname>/
  logs/0-run/
    unified_tree_viz.html      <- open in a browser; the tree, working vs buggy nodes
    journal.json / *.json      <- per-node plan, code, execution output, debug attempts
  <timestamp_ideaname>.pdf     <- exists only if the run succeeded
Quick triage commands (hand these to Claude Code):

  echo "${d}  PDF: ${pdf:-NONE}"
done
# Inside one run: find the per-node journal and count buggy vs working nodes

# then have Claude Code parse the journal: for each node print {id, parent, is_buggy,
# error type/first traceback line, n_debug_attempts, plan one-liner}
For each failure node, extract and record:
stage (Stage 1 draft? later refinement?), the node's plan (what it intended)
the code it wrote (the diff from its parent node is most informative)
the execution error (exact traceback / error class)
how many times it tried to debug (max_debug_depth) and whether it abandoned (debug_prob)
outcome: fixed → working, or abandoned
Classify each into one of three axes (this is the sharpened version of your model/task/confound
separation):
AxisSignatureExampleTask specificationIdea was vague/infeasible; agent flails on undefined choicesNo dataset/metric specified → tries random datasets, OOM, gives upModel capabilityAgent understood the task but couldn't write correct code for the methodMisimplements the actual algorithm; can't fix a subtle numerical bugTool-use strategyCould have succeeded but used tools poorly / gave up earlyMisreads traceback, re-submits same broken code, abandons after 1 debug, ignores OOM signal
Pick one or two of the richest cases for the report. The best case is one where the
classification isn't obvious and you had to look — that's the depth Taiming wants.
Part C — Controlled experiments (1–2 new runs, to test your diagnosis)
The point of a new run is to test a hypothesis from Part B, not to generate more data. Design
each as a clean A/B: same idea, same seed, change exactly one variable. Run the two best for
your specific failure cases.
#Hypothesis (axis)Change exactly one thingWhat to measureRough costE1Many failures are abandonment, not incapability (tool-use)max_debug_depth 3→8 and/or debug_prob 0.5→0.9success Y/N; # buggy nodes that become working after extra debug~$15–25E2The failure is task spec, not the agent (task spec)Rewrite idea .md: pin dataset, model size, exact metric, compute budget# OOM/setup errors; nodes-to-first-working-node; success~$15–25E3It's capability (model capability)Swap experiment model only (e.g. claude-3-5-sonnet ↔ a weaker/cheaper or stronger model), keep idea+seedsame error recurs? success Y/N~$15–25E4A correct scaffold unblocks early setup (tool-use/task)Add --load_code with a starter snippet vs withoutnodes-to-first-working-experiment~$15–25E5Breadth beats depth in open search (search design)num_drafts/num_workers 1→3how many roots succeed; diversity of approaches~$20–30
Recommended pair: E1 (tool-use) + E2 (task spec). They map cleanly onto two of the three
diagnostic axes, are the most likely to surface an actual research idea, and E2 doubles as the
CUDA-OOM fix. Add E3 only if budget allows — it's the cleanest capability isolator.
Cost control (aim for $0 via the Sandbox; the $ figures below are the paid fallback):
If the Sandbox is wired in (Part D2 / E1b), per-run cost is ~$0 — the dollar estimates in the
table above only apply if you fall back to paid OpenAI/Bedrock APIs. Even so, keep runs small.
Lower steps (e.g. 12–16) and num_drafts (1–2) for the controlled runs.
Use a cheap model for --model_citation / --model_review (e.g. gpt-4o or gpt-4o-mini).
For failure analysis you mostly care about the experiment tree, not the PDF — you can analyze
the tree the moment the experiment stage finishes; you don't have to pay for every writeup.
Reuse one generated idea JSON across the A/B so ideation cost is paid once.

Cost ($0) path — Princeton AI Sandbox. The Sandbox gives Princeton affiliates free,
unlimited LLM access via a programming API (Azure-backed; undergrads get access through a faculty
sponsor). If you can route AI-Scientist-v2's calls through it, the per-token cost in this runbook
goes to ~$0. Caveat: it's not plug-and-play — the repo expects standard OPENAI_API_KEY +
OpenAI endpoints, while the Sandbox uses AI_SANDBOX_KEY and its own Azure base URL and model
names. You'll need to point the repo's LLM client at the Sandbox base URL and use the Sandbox's
available model names. See Part E for the compute-node module + how to wire it in, and treat
"does the repo support a custom base_url cleanly?" as something to verify in the code (it's a
legitimate setup challenge to document in the report).
Note: the default bfts_config.yaml uses claude-3-5-sonnet for experiments, which needs AWS
Bedrock (pip install "anthropic[bedrock]" + AWS creds). To skip Bedrock entirely, point the
experiment model at an OpenAI/Gemini model in bfts_config.yaml (or a Sandbox model). Routing
through Gemini also lets you spend the Google Cloud free $300 credit the warmup program mentions.

Part E — Running on Adroit (SLURM) + the gotchas that will actually bite you
The warmup README says you don't need the full hardware — a MIG A100 or V100 on Adroit is fine
for small-scale runs. Verify exact partition/--gres syntax against the Princeton RC SLURM guide
and the lab's internal Della cluster-guide (the warmup repo links both).
E1 gotcha — outbound internet on compute nodes (use the proxy module).
AI-Scientist-v2 makes constant API calls, hits Semantic Scholar, and the LLM-written code may try
to download datasets/packages at runtime. Princeton RC compute nodes don't have open outbound
internet by default — you reach external endpoints (and the AI Sandbox) by loading the proxy
module on the compute node (it doesn't work on login nodes):
bashsalloc --gres=gpu:1 --time=00:30:00 --mem=16G   # adjust to Adroit's syntax
module load proxy/default
curl -sSf https://api.openai.com/v1/models >/dev/null && echo "internet OK" || echo "NO INTERNET"
If it still fails after module load proxy/default, document it (a legit setup challenge to report)
and ask RC/Taiming. Note that some traffic the LLM-written code generates may not honor the proxy
env vars — another reason to keep runs small and watched.
E1b — wiring the Princeton AI Sandbox (the $0 route).
Per Princeton RC, you access the Sandbox from cluster compute nodes with module load proxy/default
and an AI_SANDBOX_KEY. To make AI-Scientist-v2 actually use it you must point the repo's LLM
client at the Sandbox's base URL and use the Sandbox's model names instead of public OpenAI ones.
Concretely, have Claude Code do this by reading the repo's real LLM client (don't guess the
file/keys):
"Find where this repo constructs its OpenAI client (likely ai_scientist/llm.py or similar).
Show me how it sets the API key and base URL. Then add support for the Princeton Sandbox: read
AI_SANDBOX_KEY and a Sandbox base URL, and let me select Sandbox model names — without breaking
the existing OpenAI/Gemini paths."
Get the exact base URL, available model names, and key from the Princeton RC AI Sandbox page
(researchcomputing.princeton.edu/support/knowledge-base/ai-sandbox) and the sample myscript.py
it links. If the repo can't cleanly take a custom base_url, say so in the report — that's a real
finding, and you can fall back to the GCP $300 credit via Gemini.
E2 gotcha — it runs LLM-written code.
The README explicitly warns this executes arbitrary model-generated code (dangerous packages,
uncontrolled web access, spawned processes) and recommends a sandbox/Docker. Adroit gives you no
Docker (no root). Options: be conservative, run in a constrained env, or use Apptainer/Singularity
if the lab prefers. Note the Princeton AI Sandbox is a secure place to get model access, not a
sandbox for executing the agent's generated code — those are two different "sandbox" meanings, so
clarify with Taiming where the code execution itself should happen.
E3 — SLURM submission script (template — verify the #SBATCH lines for Adroit)
bash#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=ai_sci_E1
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1            # MIG A100 or V100; check Adroit's exact gres/constraint
#SBATCH --time=06:00:00         # runs take several hours; check undergrad time limits
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
module purge
module load proxy/default       # outbound internet + AI Sandbox access (compute nodes only)
module load anaconda3/2024.x    # use the module name Adroit actually provides
conda activate ai_scientist
source ~/.ai_scientist_secrets  # keys live here (incl. AI_SANDBOX_KEY), NOT in this script
cd $HOME/AI-Scientist-v2
# Point bfts_config.yaml at the variant for this experiment first, e.g.:
cp configs/E1_debug8.yaml bfts_config.yaml
python launch_scientist_bfts.py \
  --load_ideas "ai_scientist/ideas/my_topic.json" \
  --load_code --add_dataset_ref \
  --model_writeup o1-preview-2024-09-12 \
  --model_citation gpt-4o-2024-11-20 \
  --model_review gpt-4o-2024-11-20 \
  --model_agg_plots o3-mini-2025-01-31 \
  --num_cite_rounds 20
Submit with sbatch run_E1.slurm; watch with squeue -u $USER and tail -f slurm-<jobid>.out.
E4 — CUDA OOM
If you hit "CUDA Out of Memory," edit the idea .md to instruct smaller models/batch sizes for
experiments (this is the README's recommended fix, and it overlaps with experiment E2).

The runbook's commands/config snippets were slightly off from the **actual** repo, so per its own "the repo wins" rule I verified everything by reading the real source (README, `bfts_config.yaml`, `launch_scientist_bfts.py`, `llm.py`, the tree-search `backend_openai.py`, `journal.py`) and the Princeton Sandbox sample. Key corrections baked into the kit:
- `bfts_config.yaml` is **nested** (e.g. `agent.search.max_debug_depth`), not the flat keys the runbook lists; real defaults are `num_workers: 4` (not 3) and per-stage `stageN_max_iters` (no single `steps: 21`).
- The **$0 Sandbox route needs a real code patch**: the repo builds bare `openai.OpenAI()` clients in *two* places, and the Sandbox is Azure-flavored (`AzureOpenAI` + `api_version`), so a base_url alone won't do it. The default experiment model is also Bedrock-Claude, which bypasses OpenAI entirely — so you must also swap it. Both handled.

- **`ideas/`** — E2's vague vs. pinned idea files (CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 small enough for a MIG slice).
- **`slurm/`** — `run_E1.slurm`, `run_E2.slurm`.

## What was happening (you weren't doing anything wrong — the kit's assumptions were)

Your live test exposed that **Adroit's network is the reverse of what the kit assumed**:

- **Login node** (`adroit-vis`) → general internet. Your `git clone` succeeded there.
- **Compute node** → no general internet; `module load proxy/default` only opens a small **allowlist**. That's why github gave `403` and the clone failed there.

Plus three smaller real bugs the run surfaced: `module load anaconda3` needs a pinned version, conda's activate trips `set -u` (`PS1: unbound variable`), and there's no `mig` partition (GPUs live in `gpu`, MIG slices are `gres 3g.20gb` — confirmed by your own `snodes`).

**The one thing that is *not* a bug:** the Sandbox `502`. github got `403` (blocked); the Sandbox got `502` (reached, but `/` isn't a valid endpoint). Different code = the Sandbox host is most likely allow-listed from compute nodes. A bare `curl /` can never prove it — only a real `chat.completions.create` can.

## Fixes pushed (just `git pull` on the branch)

- `setup_adroit.sh` → runs on the **login node**, refuses to run where github is blocked, pins the anaconda module, sources `conda.sh`, fixes the `PS1` issue, puts repo+env on scratch.
- Both SLURM scripts → `--partition=gpu --gres=gpu:3g.20gb:1`, conda-activate fix, and a **real AzureOpenAI smoke test** that aborts the job early if the Sandbox is genuinely unreachable (so you don't waste a GPU slot).
- New **login-node dataset pre-fetch** step (step 4b) — compute nodes can't download CIFAR-10 at runtime.
- Secrets template now exports `REPO_DIR`/`CONDA_ENVS_DIR`/`CIFAR_DIR`/`HF_HOME` on scratch.
- `report.md` Part E + troubleshooting table document all of it (the topology is itself a finding the runbook asked you to record).

## Your unblock path right now (on the login node `adroit-vis`)

```bash
cd /scratch/network/$USER/zlab-training/ai-scientist-v2 && git pull
export REPO_DIR=/scratch/network/$USER/AI-Scientist-v2
export CONDA_ENVS_DIR=/scratch/network/$USER/conda-envs
export ANACONDA_MODULE=anaconda3/2024.6
bash scripts/setup_adroit.sh          # clone + env, all on scratch
```

Then secrets → `wire_sandbox.py` → run the **Sandbox smoke test from inside a `salloc --partition=gpu` session** (steps 2–3 of `experiments.md`). That smoke test is the real go/no-go for the whole $0 plan — if it returns "sandbox OK" from a compute node, you're clear to submit E1/E2; if it fails, that's the finding to take to RC (ask them to allowlist `api-ai-sandbox.princeton.edu` for compute nodes).

Want me to also add a tiny standalone `scripts/check_sandbox.py` you can run by itself on a compute node, so you can confirm reachability before committing to a full job?

### ASSISTANT

That's your **secrets file** — the private copy of the template, holding your API keys. It's not tracked by git (that's intentional). But two things need fixing before it'll work:

**1. You accidentally pasted a command into the top of the file.** Line 1 currently reads:

```
source ~/.ai_scientist_secrets# Copy to ~/.ai_scientist_secrets...
```

That `source ~/.ai_scientist_secrets` at the very start is a shell command that got typed *into* the file. Delete it so line 1 starts with `# Copy to...`. (If left in, sourcing the file would try to source itself.)

**2. Paste your real Sandbox key.** Change this line:

```
export AI_SANDBOX_KEY="PASTE_YOUR_SANDBOX_KEY"
```

…replacing `PASTE_YOUR_SANDBOX_KEY` with your actual key from the [AI Sandbox page](https://researchcomputing.princeton.edu/support/knowledge-base/ai-sandbox) (the web chat interface has a "API key" section, or request one there).

**Then:**
- Save and exit nano: `Ctrl+O`, `Enter`, `Ctrl+X`
- Back at the shell prompt (not inside nano), run: `source ~/.ai_scientist_secrets`

That's what loads `AI_SANDBOX_KEY`, `USE_AI_SANDBOX=1`, and the scratch paths into your shell so the scripts can use them.

Everything else in the file is fine as-is — the `OPENAI_API_KEY="[REDACTED]"` dummy is deliberate (it makes any unpatched code path fail loudly instead of silently hitting paid OpenAI), and the commented-out blocks are optional things you don't need for the $0 Sandbox route.

Quick check after sourcing — this should print your key and `1`:

```bash
echo "${AI_SANDBOX_KEY:0:6}...  USE_AI_SANDBOX=$USE_AI_SANDBOX"
```

### ASSISTANT

Setup is 95% there — env built on scratch, all pip packages in. Just **one known issue** hit at the very end:

```
ImportError: .../libtorch_cpu.so: undefined symbol: iJIT_NotifyEvent
```

This is a classic conda gotcha: the solver pulled **MKL 2025**, which removed the `iJIT_NotifyEvent` symbol that PyTorch 2.5.1 links against. Fix = downgrade MKL to 2024. There's also a minor `sympy` version mismatch pip warned about (torch wants `1.13.1`, got `1.14.0`). Both are quick fixes.

## Run this now (on the login node)

```bash
module load anaconda3/2024.6
source "$(conda info --base)/etc/profile.d/conda.sh"
conda activate ai_scientist

conda install -n ai_scientist "mkl=2024.0" -y     # fixes iJIT_NotifyEvent
pip install "sympy==1.13.1"                        # matches what torch 2.5.1 wants

python -c "import torch; print('torch', torch.__version__, 'cuda', torch.cuda.is_available())"
```

That should now print `torch 2.5.1 cuda False` — **`False` is correct on the login node** (no GPU here); the real CUDA check happens inside the GPU job. The thing that matters is that `import torch` no longer crashes.

Let me bake both pins into `setup_adroit.sh` so you (and anyone pulling the kit) don't hit this again:

from mimetypes import guess_type

[REDACTED] Import API key from OS environment variables

sandbox_api_version = "2025-03-01-preview"

                    "gpt-4o-mini",
                    "gpt-4o",
                    "gpt-35-turbo-16k",

                    "Meta-Llama-3-1-8B-Instruct-nwxcg",
                    "Mistral-small-zgjes"]
 
# Base 64 encode local image and return text to be included in JSON request
def local_image_to_data_url(image_path):
    """
    Get the url of a local image
    """
    mime_type, _ = guess_type(image_path)
 
    if mime_type is None:
        mime_type = "application/octet-stream"
 
    with open(image_path, "rb") as image_file:
        base64_encoded_data = base64.b64encode(image_file.read()).decode("utf-8")
 
    return f"data:{mime_type};base64,{base64_encoded_data}"


# This function will submit a simple text prompt to the chosen model
def text_prompt_example(model_to_be_used):
    # Establish a connection to your Azure OpenAI instance
    client = AzureOpenAI(
        api_key=sandbox_api_key,
        azure_endpoint = sandbox_endpoint,
        api_version=sandbox_api_version # current api version not in preview
    )
 
    # temperature = how creative/random the model is in generating response;
    #               0 to 1 with 1 being most creative
    # max_tokens = token limit on context to send to the model
    # top_p = diversity of generated text by the model considering probability
    #         attached to token; 0 to 1 - ex. top_p of 0.1 = only tokens within
    #         the top 10% probability are considered
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
               model=model_to_be_used,
               temperature=0.5, 
               max_tokens=1000, 
               top_p=0.5,
               messages=[
                         {"role": "system",
                          "content": "You are a helpful junior physics professor."},
                         {"role": "user",
                          "content": "Please explain quantum mechanics in 100 words or less."},
                         ])
 
    print("\n"+response.choices[0].message.content)
 
# This function will ask the model to describe what is in the given image
# NOTE:  I tried using the client.chat.completions.create() function for this, 
# but it resulted in HTTP 431 "Too many headers" errors.
# In order to reduce the number of HTTP headers I switched to 
# submitting JSON directly to the API using a requests.post() function.
def image_prompt_example(model_to_be_used, image_file):
    headers = {
               'api-key': sandbox_api_key,
               'Content-Type': 'application/json'
              }
 
    data = {
             "messages": [{"role": "system",
                           "content": "You are a helpful assistant to analyse images."},
                          {"role": "user",
                           "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?"},
                          {"type": "image_url",
                           "image_url": {"url":local_image_to_data_url(image_file)}}]}],
             "model": model_to_be_used,
             "max_tokens": 2000,
             "temperature": 0.0
            }
 
    # Generate JSON object
    try:
        # Convert dictionary to JSON string
        json_data = json.dumps(data)
        # Parse JSON string to validate
        parsed_data = json.loads(json_data)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        print("Invalid JSON, unable to create JSON object:", e)
        exit(-1)
 
    endpoint = sandbox_endpoint + "openai/deployments/" + \
               model_to_be_used + "/chat/completions?api-version=" + \
               sandbox_api_version
 
    response = requests.post(endpoint, data=json_data, headers=headers)
    #print(response.text)
 
    json_response = json.loads(response.text)
    print("\n"+json_response['choices'][0]['message']['content'])

Using the A.I. Sandbox from the Research Computing Clusters
The chat and API workloads of the Sandbox are executed using cloud resources. This is sufficient for the majority of Sandbox users. One can also combine the Sandbox with the high-performance computing resources of Research Computing.
Special access to the A.I. Sandbox from the compute nodes of the Research Computing clusters is made available by loading the following [environment module](https://researchcomputing.princeton.edu/support/knowledge-base/modules):

```
module load proxy/default
```

Note that this module can only be used on compute nodes (not login nodes). Learn more about the [proxy/default module](https://researchcomputing.princeton.edu/support/knowledge-base/ports-and-proxydefault). Here is a  Slurm script example of running a Python code that uses the Sandbox from the Research Computing clusters:

```
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=sandbox          # create a short name for your job
#SBATCH --nodes=1                   # node count
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                  # total number of tasks across all nodes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1           # cpu-cores per task (>1 if multi-threaded tasks)
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G            # memory per cpu-core (4G per cpu-core is default)
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00             # total run time limit (HH:MM:SS)
#SBATCH --mail-type=begin,end,fail  # send email when job begins

module purge
module load proxy/default
module load anaconda3/2025.12
conda activate myenv

export AI_SANDBOX_KEY=[REDACTED] provided to you>

python myscript.py

```

**That's the difference** — your working code uses `api_version = "2024-02-01"`, and `token_usage.py` literally comments *"current api version not in preview"*. We've been using `2025-03-01-preview` (from the newer myscript.py example). Same endpoint, same client, same key — only the api_version differs.

This could absolutely cause the 502: Adroit's proxy appears to **terminate TLS** (it's a filtering proxy, not a plain tunnel), so the request path — including `?api-version=...` — actually reaches the upstream through the proxy. A bad/unsupported api_version can come back as a 502 rather than a clean 4xx. Your proven value is the thing to test.

Quickest test — point the kit's env var at your known-good api_version and re-run the check job:

```bash
# set your proven api_version in secrets
sed -i 's|SANDBOX_API_VERSION=.*|SANDBOX_API_VERSION="2024-02-01"|' ~/.ai_scientist_secrets
grep SANDBOX_API_VERSION ~/.ai_scientist_secrets        # confirm it changed
source ~/.ai_scientist_secrets

cd /scratch/network/$USER/zlab-training/ai-scientist-v2
sbatch slurm/check_sandbox.slurm
# wait ~20s, then read the NEWEST output (highest job number):
ls -t sbx-*.out | head -1 | xargs cat
```

(The check script reads `SANDBOX_API_VERSION` from your secrets, and uses `gpt-4o-mini`, which is in your anuta model list — so this is an apples-to-apples test against your known-good setup.)

- If it prints `sandbox says: ok` → **the Sandbox is back**, the only bug was the api_version. I'll change the kit's default to `2024-02-01` and we resume the $0-Sandbox plan (no Gemini needed).
- If it *still* 502s with `2024-02-01` → then the Sandbox really is down/changed since your anuta runs, and Gemini is the move.

### ASSISTANT

Still failing after the conda reinstall — so this is a conda torch↔torchvision ABI mismatch that the `mkl=2024` downgrade made worse (it pulled `libstdc++` back a version, breaking torchvision's compiled ops). Fighting it inside conda is a losing game. The reliable fix is to **replace the conda torch stack with PyTorch's self-contained pip cu124 wheels** — those are mutually ABI-matched, bundle their own libs, and don't depend on conda's `mkl`/`libstdc++` at all (so neither the `iJIT` nor the `nms` error can recur):

```bash
conda remove -n ai_scientist --force-remove pytorch torchvision torchaudio pytorch-cuda -y
pip install --no-cache-dir torch==2.5.1 torchvision==0.20.1 torchaudio==2.5.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124
python -c "import torch, torchvision; print('torch', torch.__version__, 'tv', torchvision.__version__, 'cuda', torch.cuda.is_available())"
```

Expect `torch 2.5.1 tv 0.20.1 cuda False` (False is fine on login). The pip wheels download from `download.pytorch.org`, which the login node can reach.

If that prints both versions cleanly, immediately re-cache CIFAR and we're past the env wall:
```bash
python -c "import torchvision as tv,os; r=os.environ['CIFAR_DIR']; tv.datasets.CIFAR10(r,train=True,download=True); tv.datasets.CIFAR10(r,train=False,download=True); print('CIFAR cached at',r)"
```

Paste the version line. Once torchvision imports, I'll switch `setup_adroit.sh` to use these pip wheels (so the conda/mkl trap is gone for good), and then you launch the E2 run.

```bash
cd /scratch/network/$USER/zlab-training/ai-scientist-v2 && git pull

mkdir -p $REPO_DIR/configs
COMMON="--set agent.code.model=gpt-4o-mini --set agent.feedback.model=gpt-4o-mini --set agent.vlm_feedback.model=gpt-4o-mini --set report.model=gpt-4o-mini"
python scripts/apply_experiment_config.py --config $REPO_DIR/bfts_config.yaml --preset baseline --small $COMMON --out $REPO_DIR/configs/E2_baseline.yaml
```

**2. Launch E2 / concrete** (CIFAR is cached, so the agent's code can actually run):
```bash
cd $REPO_DIR
cp /scratch/network/$USER/zlab-training/ai-scientist-v2/slurm/run_E2.slurm .
IDEA=ai_scientist/ideas/topic_concrete.json sbatch run_E2.slurm
squeue -u $USER
```

**3. Watch it:**
```bash
tail -f slurm-<jobid>.out
```

What to expect — this is the real AI-Scientist-v2 launcher running end to end for the first time, so:
- The job's first action is the OpenAI pre-flight (`openai OK: ok`), then it copies the E2 config over `bfts_config.yaml` and starts the tree search.
- It'll churn for a while (Stage 1 drafting → running nodes). The agent writes code, executes it on the MIG GPU, and the journal fills with working/buggy nodes — **that's your failure-analysis data**.
- A repo-specific surprise (a path, a config key, an arg) is still possible on first contact. If it crashes early, paste the first real traceback from `slurm-<jobid>.out` and we fix it. If it starts producing nodes, let it run.

Paste the first ~40 lines of `slurm-<jobid>.out` once it's running (or the error if it stops early), and we'll either keep watching or debug.

KB0014563
AI Sandbox FAQ
Article metadata.
This article was updated about a month agoabout a month ago
 This article has 457 views.•  457 Views

1. Who can access the AI Sandbox? The AI Sandbox is available to Princeton faculty conducting academic research. Faculty members may request access for themselves or others they supervise using the [AI Sandbox Access Request Form](https://princeton.service-now.com/service?id=sc_cat_item&table=sc_cat_item&sys_id=dca54d1c1b495690423c777b1d4bcb94&searchTerm=AI%20Sandbox%20form). 
2. How do I get access to the AI Sandbox? Access to the AI Sandbox is granted through an approval process. It typically takes up to two (2) business days from the request to have your account set up and ready.
3. How soon can I access the AI Sandbox web interface after my account is set up? Once your account is set up, it typically takes about an hour for permissions to propagate, after which you can access the AI Sandbox web interface.
4. What do I need to use the AI Sandbox programmatically? You will be issued an API key to access the AI Sandbox programmatically. Once you have the key, you can run your code from anywhere with the appropriate credentials.  Here are examples for using Python to use the API:  [portkey_text_example.py](https://princeton.service-now.com/sys_attachment.do?sys_id=5241b4f387704b58731f322d0ebb35fa) and [portkey_image_example.py](https://princeton.service-now.com/sys_attachment.do?sys_id=d241b4f387704b58731f322d0ebb35f6)
5. What is "Portkey"? [Portkey](https://portkey.ai/) is the AI API Gateway service that we use to route your prompt to the appropriate LLM.  Portkey allows us to manage user access, track token costs associated with each user and limit monthly costs.  Unfortunately each user cannot request a report of their monthly spend, however we understand that Portkey is planning to provide this functionality in future versions.
6. Can I use AI Sandbox with Claude Code? Yes.  You can configure the Claude Code application to connect to AI Sandbox for access to LLM’s.  See the Portkey Information on Claude Code Integration.  The following is an example entry for the ~/.claude/settings.json file: 

```
{ 
   
	"theme": "light", 
   

"env": {"ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://api.portkey.ai", 
    "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "<MY PORTKEY API KEY>", 
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-4-6", 
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "claude-opus-4-7", 
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "claude-haiku-4-5" 
  }, 

"model": "claude-sonnet-4-6" 
 

} 
```

7. What models are available in the AI Sandbox? The models available in the AI Sandbox change over time. For the most up-to-date information on available models, please refer to the AI Sandbox KB article: [AI Sandbox Overview](https://kb.princeton.edu/KB0014337).
8. What API methods are supported in the AI Sandbox? The AI Sandbox currently supports the openai.ChatCompletion.create method, which is part of the earlier OpenAI SDK approach. The Responses API from the newer SDK is not yet supported and attempts to use this may result in a 404 error.
9. Can I send multiple API calls at the same time in the AI Sandbox? Yes, you can send simultaneous API calls using parallel processing methods such as Python multiprocessing. However, be mindful of rate limits and potential costs associated with high-volume requests. Rates are listed please in the AI Sandbox KB article: [AI Sandbox Overview](https://kb.princeton.edu/KB0014337).
10. Is there a cost to using the AI Sandbox? The AI Sandbox is available with a $250/month budget cap per user. If your usage exceeds this limit, access to the Sandbox will be temporarily restricted until the following month, when the budget resets.
11. How do I manage costs when using the AI Sandbox? The AI Sandbox has a $250/month budget cap per user. If your usage exceeds this limit, access to the Sandbox will be temporarily restricted until the following month. If you anticipate needing to exceed this cap, please provide OIT with a project chart string for billing the additional charges. This ensures that costs are appropriately tracked and billed.
12. What should I do if my AI Sandbox request is blocked by content safety filtering? If content filtering interferes with your work, please review your prompt to ensure it doesn’t trigger the safety filters. If the issue persists, contact the [AI Sandbox support team](mailto:cses@princeton.edu?subject=AI%20Sandbox%20Question) for guidance on adjusting your prompt or exploring alternative solutions. Content filtering is enabled to ensure responsible use of the platform.
13. Is it possible to disable content filtering in the AI Sandbox? Currently, content filtering cannot be disabled in the AI Sandbox, as it is in place to prevent harmful content and ensure compliance with university policies. This decision follows guidance from the Dean for Research, and we are not able to remove or bypass these filters at this time.
14. How do I report an error in the AI Sandbox? If you encounter errors, such as content filtering issues or technical glitches, please reach out to the [AI Sandbox support team](mailto:cses@princeton.edu?subject=AI%20Sandbox%20Error) with details of the error message, model used, and the task performed.
15. Can the AI Sandbox support research outside of faculty work? The AI Sandbox is currently designed to support faculty research and students sponsored by faculty. 
16. Can I collaborate with other Princeton researches on a project using the AI Sandbox? Yes, the AI Sandbox allows faculty members to collaborate on research projects, but each individual will need to have their own access credentials. You can work with your team members and share resources accordingly.
17. Can I access the AI Sandbox from a computing node? Yes, you can access the AI Sandbox from computing nodes. Once you have been granted access and issued API keys, you can run your code remotely, including from computing nodes within Princeton's network. Additional details - [A.I. Sandbox | Princeton Research Computing](https://researchcomputing.princeton.edu/support/knowledge-base/ai-sandbox)
18. What should I do if I need to scale my API usage or use a larger model? If your project requires more resources or if you anticipate exceeding the cap, please contact us with your project chart string for billing the difference. We’ll discuss potential solutions to accommodate your needs within budget constraints.
19. Does the AI Sandbox support any AI agent toolboxes, like LangChain or Semantic Kernel? The AI Sandbox is primarily designed to support LLM's for general-purpose research. Advanced frameworks such as LangChain and Semantic Kernel are not currently integrated into the system but may be available through other means. Please contact the [AI support team](mailto:cses@princeton.edu?subject=AI%20Sandbox%20Question) if you need assistance with specific toolboxes.
20. What happens when a model retires? When a model retires, it will no longer be available for use in the AI Sandbox. We periodically update the [AI Sandbox article](https://princeton.service-now.com/service?id=kb_article&sys_id=KB0014337) to reflect the status of models, including any retirements, new model availability, and associated costs. Please check the article regularly for the latest information.
21. How can I optimize performance when using the AI Sandbox? To ensure optimal performance when using the AI Sandbox, it’s important to consider factors like model selection, input size, and request frequency. ### ASSISTANT

**This is real, classifiable data — and the pattern is striking.** All 14 nodes buggy, and the error breakdown:

```
7  URLError            <- the agent's code tried to DOWNLOAD CIFAR-10 at runtime
3  ModuleNotFoundError <- imported a package not in the env
2  SystemExit
1  NameError
1  FileNotFoundError
```

**Finding #1 (and it's a good one): half of all Stage-1 failures are an *environment confound*, not agent incapability.** `URLError` is the agent writing `CIFAR10(root='./data', download=True)` — which hits the blocked network on the compute node (no general internet), exactly the wall we've been fighting. The agent *can't* succeed at a data-loading task when the data path it chose requires a download the cluster forbids. That's the runbook's "confound" in the flesh: on a restricted cluster, a big chunk of "agent failure" is really infrastructure.

To turn this into a *clean* test of the three diagnostic axes, we remove that confound (pre-stage the data where the agent's code will find it offline) and re-run — then whatever fails next is genuine agent signal.

First, confirm the URLError really is the CIFAR download, and grab the node schema so I can fix the miner's parent/debug-depth columns (they read blank — the journal stores parent under a different key). One command:

```bash
python - <<'PY'
import json
p="experiments/2026-06-29_13-18-30_regularization_backfire_cifar_attempt_0/logs/0-run/stage_1_initial_implementation_1_preliminary/journal.json"
d=json.load(open(p)); ns=d["nodes"] if isinstance(d,dict) else d
n=ns[0]
print("KEYS:", list(n.keys()))
print("PARENT:", repr(n.get("parent")), " CHILDREN:", repr(n.get("children"))[:80])
to=n.get("_term_out") or n.get("term_out") or ""
to="".join(map(str,to)) if isinstance(to,list) else to
print("TERM_OUT TAIL:\n", to[-1200:])
PY
```

Paste that. Then the fix is: stage CIFAR into the framework's `data_dir` (which it copies into every node workspace, so `download=True` finds it and skips the network), set `generate_report=false` (kills that end-of-run crash), and re-launch. We're now genuinely doing the experiment — first run already produced a documentable finding.

Now the cleanup-and-rerun to remove the download confound and get genuine agent signal. On the login node (you're in `$REPO_DIR`):

**1. Stage CIFAR where the framework hands data to every node** (so `download=True` finds it and skips the network):
```bash
mkdir -p $REPO_DIR/data
cp -r /scratch/network/$USER/data/cifar-10-batches-py $REPO_DIR/data/
ls $REPO_DIR/data/cifar-10-batches-py | head
```

**2. Pull the miner fix + rebuild the config** — stronger coder (`gpt-4o` instead of `mini`, since weak-coder noise muddies the signal) and `generate_report=false` (kills that end-of-run crash):
```bash
cd /scratch/network/$USER/zlab-training/ai-scientist-v2 && git pull
COMMON="--set agent.code.model=gpt-4o --set agent.feedback.model=gpt-4o-mini --set agent.vlm_feedback.model=gpt-4o-mini --set report.model=gpt-4o-mini --set generate_report=false"
python scripts/apply_experiment_config.py --config $REPO_DIR/bfts_config.yaml --preset baseline --small $COMMON --out $REPO_DIR/configs/E2_baseline.yaml
```

**3. Re-launch E2/concrete:**
```bash
cd $REPO_DIR
IDEA=ai_scientist/ideas/topic_concrete.json sbatch run_E2.slurm
squeue -u $USER
```

Why this should change the picture: CIFAR is now staged in both places the agent's code is likely to look (`./data` via the framework's workspace staging, and `$CIFAR_DIR` via the idea instruction + the run script's export), so the 7 `URLError` nodes should vanish. Whatever fails *now* is real agent signal — coding bugs, wrong APIs, debug-loop behavior — which is what E1 (debug depth) and the three-axis classification actually study.

When it finishes (watch `tail -f slurm-<jobid>.out`), mine it the same way — and the directory form now works thanks to the recursive fix:
```bash
python /scratch/network/$USER/zlab-training/ai-scientist-v2/scripts/mine_journal.py \
  experiments/<new_run>/logs/0-run/ -o E2_clean_nodes.csv
```

Paste the new mining summary + table. If `URLError` is gone and you see a mix of real coding errors (and hopefully a working node or two), we've got the clean dataset — and the contrast between this run and the confounded one is a great two-row result for the report. Then we do E1 (debug depth 3→8) on the same idea.

self.task_desc
You are an ambitious AI researcher who is looking to publish a paper that will 
contribute significantly to the field.
You have an idea and you want to conduct creative experiments to gain scientific
insights.
Your aim is to run experiments to gather sufficient results for a top conference
paper.
Your research idea:


Title:
When Regularization Backfires: A Controlled Study on CIFAR-10 with a Small CNN
Abstract:
Practitioners reach for dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and label 
smoothing whenever data is scarce, assuming these techniques improve 
generalization. In practice the picture is murkier: some regularizers leave a 
model worse off than a plain baseline. We isolate when this happens under a 
fully specified, reproducible protocol designed to run on a single ~10GB GPU. We
use CIFAR-10 with a FIXED 5,000-image training subset (500 per class, seed 0) 
and the full 10,000-image test set, and a ResNet-18 trained from scratch (no 
pretrained weights). We compare a no-regularization baseline against four 
one-variable-at-a-time conditions: dropout p=0.3, weight decay 5e-4, label 
smoothing 0.1, and RandAugment. The metric is top-1 test accuracy, reported as 
mean +/- std over 3 seeds (0,1,2). Training is fixed: SGD, lr=0.1 
cosine-decayed, batch size 128, 30 epochs, no early stopping, no hyperparameter 
search. The deliverable is a table of test accuracy per arm and seed plus a bar 
chart with error bars, identifying which arms fall below baseline and by how 
much.
Short Hypothesis:
On a fixed small CIFAR-10 subset trained with a fixed ResNet-18 from scratch 
under an identical modest budget, some standard regularizers (dropout, weight 
decay, label smoothing, RandAugment) reduce top-1 test accuracy below an 
unregularized baseline. Pinning the setup reveals exactly which regularizers 
backfire and by how much.

**Stop it now — Ctrl-C.** It's stuck in an infinite loop burning your OpenAI credits, but here's the thing: **it actually worked.** Look at node 0 in every line:

```
[0, None, '2af67383...', False, False]   ← is_buggy = False = a WORKING node
```

The agent trained ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 on your GPU and got **real results** — `941b8c8b…` hit **28.61% validation accuracy**, others 23.74%, 17%, etc. **The full pipeline ran end-to-end.** That's the clean success we've been chasing for hours.

**Why it's now looping:** it got all the way to **Stage 4 (ablation studies)**, where each node trains *several* models. Those need more than the **120-second** `exec.timeout` I set to dodge the WSL hang — so every Stage-4 node times out → marked buggy → the search keeps retrying forever. That 120s cap saved us from the deadlock but is too short for the heavy ablation nodes. (That's itself a clean finding.)

So: **Ctrl-C**, then mine the run — you now have working *and* buggy nodes with real metrics:

## Adroit — same idea, three differences

The *concept* is identical (run `collect_outputs.sh`, commit, push), but three things change on Adroit:

**1. Do it all on the LOGIN node.** Compute nodes have no internet, so `git push` only works from the login node (`ssh` in normally, don't `salloc`).

**2. Different paths.** Your zlab-training clone and the experiments dir are elsewhere on Adroit. Find them first:

```bash
# find your zlab-training checkout
ls -d ~/zlab-training 2>/dev/null || find ~ /scratch/network/$USER -maxdepth 3 -name zlab-training -type d 2>/dev/null
# find the AI-Scientist experiments output
ls -dt /scratch/network/$USER/AI-Scientist-v2/experiments/*/ 2>/dev/null || ls -dt ~/AI-Scientist-v2/experiments/*/ 2>/dev/null
```

**3. Python needs the conda env** (same `python: command not found` you hit). Load it so mining works — or skip it, since I can mine here like I just did.

Then, filling in the two paths from step 2:

```bash
cd <your zlab-training checkout>
git pull origin claude/ai-scientist-v2-failures-l9vej5     # get the collector script

module load anaconda3/2024.6 && conda activate ai_scientist   # so python works (optional)

cd ai-scientist-v2
EXPROOT=<the experiments dir> WHERE=adroit bash data/collect_outputs.sh

cd <your zlab-training checkout>
git add ai-scientist-v2/data/adroit
git commit -m "data: raw adroit run output (journals + CSVs)"
git push origin claude/ai-scientist-v2-failures-l9vej5
```

Credentials: same GitHub token as your PC. Run `git config --global credential.helper store` first so it only asks once.

**Before you start**, run just the two `ls` commands from step 2 and paste them — that tells us (a) where your zlab clone is on Adroit, and (b) whether the R1/R2/R3 experiment dirs still exist on scratch (they may have been cleaned). No point running the collector if scratch got wiped. Once you push, I'll mine the Adroit journals and then both halves of the report are backed by real files.

## What this report is even about

The warmup program is: **pick an open-source ML repo, run it yourself, write up how it works and what you saw.** Last time that repo was AI-Scientist-v2 (an AI *agent* that writes papers). This time it's **Diffusers** — HuggingFace's library for **diffusion models**, the technology behind image generators like Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Midjourney.

**What a diffusion model does, in one breath:** take a real image, add a little random noise over and over until it's pure static — that's the easy "forward" direction. Then train a neural network (a U-Net) to *undo* one step of that noising. Once it can denoise, you start from pure random static and run the network backwards many times → it "hallucinates" a brand-new image that looks like your training data. That's **DDPM** (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model), the foundational algorithm.

**What you'll actually do:** train a small DDPM from scratch on ~1000 butterfly photos, watch the loss drop and the samples turn from static into blurry-then-recognizable butterflies over epochs, and document how the pieces (`UNet2DModel` = the denoiser, `DDPMScheduler` = the noise schedule, `DDPMPipeline` = the sampler) fit together. The **point** is the same as last week: understand a class of ML system by running one end-to-end — except this one is a generative model you drive directly, not a flaky agent you diagnose.
